storylines.title: The warning existed in the satellite data. There was just nobody watching it in real time
storylines.observation: A glacial lake high in the Himalayas drained on Aug 26, sending a 100km wall of water through Nepal and Tibet — now Nepal's deadliest disaster since the 2015 earthquake, with precursor signs confirmed in satellite imagery days before it happened.
storylines.question: What is the difference between a hazard being unpredictable and a hazard nobody was watching for?
storylines.hidden_question: If the data existed, was this a natural disaster or an infrastructure failure wearing one's face?
storylines.pattern: a warning that existed in the data but not in any system built to notice it
storylines.why_now: Official evening figures now put the toll at 1,358 dead and 5,326 missing - the missing count rising again rather than falling in a straight line, even as 21,146 security personnel remain mobilized and helicopters ran 112 flights in a single day. The accounting is not settling into a clean downward curve.

history.note: Official evening figures: 1,358 dead, 5,326 missing - the missing count rising again rather than falling in a straight line. 21,146 security personnel remain mobilized; helicopters ran 112 flights in a single day.

Ten days on, rescuers pulled a third worker alive from a hydropower tunnel and found a 60-year-old woman alive in flood debris in Nuwakot - survivors still emerging even as the disaster moves into its accounting phase.

NDRRMA puts a preliminary number on the damage: ~Rs 387.5 billion (~$2.8B) in losses, with Rs 8 billion needed just for the next four months of restoration - the accounting phase now running alongside a missing count still near 4,500.

Ten days on: 1,344 dead, ~4,900 still missing in Nepal (down from 5,083), 13,000+ rescued - now officially Nepal's deadliest disaster since the 2015 earthquake. Two-thirds of missing hydropower workers were at one site, Upper Trishuli-1.

storylines.title: A telescope built to find what we don't have a name for yet
storylines.observation: NASA's Roman Space Telescope, launched Aug 30 with a mirror the size of Hubble's but surveying roughly a hundred times more sky per shot, is now deep in a deliberate one-instrument-at-a-time commissioning sequence on its way to the Sun-Earth L2 point.
storylines.question: What do you build when the thing you're looking for doesn't have a name yet?
storylines.hidden_question: Is breadth or depth the better strategy for finding something genuinely unexpected?
storylines.pattern: wide-survey instrument built to catch what narrow ones would miss
storylines.why_now: No reporting has moved past the Sept 1 coronagraph power-on across three consecutive checks - the mission is now in a genuinely quiet calibration period, with the next real milestone (the Wide Field Instrument powering on) still roughly two weeks out. Going dormant rather than re-bumping the same fact a fourth time; worth reactivating when that instrument powers on.

history.note: The Coronagraph Instrument itself powered on Sept 1 - a planet-imager built to block starlight and see faint reflected light from orbiting planets - and now begins months of calibration ahead of first images expected in early 2027.

storylines.title: Armenia jails its most prominent opposition leader the day after declaring for Europe
storylines.observation: Armenian prosecutors detained former president and opposition-bloc leader Robert Kocharyan on corruption charges one day after PM Pashinyan announced Armenia's EU membership bid — raising the question of whether the case is accountability or a rival cleared from the board at a pivotal moment.
storylines.question: How do you tell an anti-corruption prosecution from a political purge when both can look identical from the outside?
storylines.hidden_question: Does the timing itself become evidence, even when the underlying charges might be entirely legitimate?
storylines.pattern: a legal crackdown landing at the exact moment it most benefits the government's freedom of maneuver
storylines.why_now: Kocharyan's own lawyer now says the case will be appealed to international courts - the ECHR or a UN body - internationalizing a fight that started as a domestic corruption case. His team frames this as a mandatory legal step, not an escalation, but it puts Armenia's judiciary itself in front of outside scrutiny.
storylines.season_or_time_context: ahead of Armenia's EU accession push

history.note: Kocharyan's lawyer says the case will be appealed to international courts - the ECHR or a UN body - calling it a mandatory step rather than an escalation. Either way, it puts Armenia's judiciary in front of outside scrutiny.

Putin broke his own usual practice and skipped congratulating Pashinyan on his June election win - a quiet snub - as Pashinyan now insists Armenia can pursue EU rapprochement while staying in the EAEU, a framing Moscow has never accepted.

Kocharyan issued a message from prison warning "this must come to an end, or everyone should start learning Turkish," accusing Armenians of losing their collective self-preservation instinct - his own voice entering the fight for the first time since detention.

storylines.title: The shutdown that 'never happened' just started happening
storylines.observation: A quarter of the world's seaborne oil passes through the Strait of Hormuz, a chokepoint whose threatened closure markets spent months pricing as leverage rather than reality — until Iran and the US resumed exchanging fire and tankers started getting hit.
storylines.question: What happens to a risk premium once the risk it was pricing actually starts happening?
storylines.hidden_question: Is the strait's value as leverage greater than its value as a functioning waterway — and does that math change once ships are actually getting struck?
storylines.pattern: a priced-in threat crossing over into the event it was pricing
storylines.why_now: Al Jazeera's own tracking now shows Hormuz traffic falling - at the same moment the US is insisting the waterway is "fully open." That's not two sides disputing a number anymore; it's one side's own headline metric moving in the opposite direction from its official claim.

history.note: Independent tracking now shows Hormuz traffic falling, at the same moment the US insists the waterway is "fully open" - not a dispute over a number anymore, but one side's own headline metric moving opposite its official claim.

Iran's parliament speaker declared "the era of 'proportionate responses' is over" - a deliberate break from the tit-for-tat framing both sides had used, as Tehran separately accuses Canada of backing Washington's push to reopen the strait by force.

Iran says it will declare an "exclusion zone" outside the strait to stop unauthorized vessels, even as a safe-passage deal with Oman nears completion. Brent hit a 7-week high near $97; US gas prices set a Labor Day record.

Iran fired a ballistic missile at US warships patrolling near the strait - experts call it a "calculated escalation," a step up from tanker strikes to a weapon aimed directly at US naval assets rather than commercial shipping.

The US struck and sank three Iranian oil tankers Saturday; IRGC claims it hit three US-affiliated vessels and three tankers back. Iran's parliament speaker warns of a "faster, heavier" response - the exchange is escalating again, not cooling.

storylines.title: The rebels declared the epidemic over in their territory. It just came back
storylines.observation: M23 rebels declared DRC's Ebola outbreak finished in their eastern Congo territory in late June; in early September a new case surfaced in rebel-held Kayna, North Kivu, in a patient who had just traveled from adjacent government-held Butembo.
storylines.question: What does it mean to declare an epidemic over in a place your own surveillance can't fully see into?
storylines.hidden_question: Was the outbreak actually contained, or did the conflict just stop anyone from checking?
storylines.pattern: a declared resolution disproven by exactly the kind of case its own blind spot couldn't catch
storylines.why_now: The national count has kept climbing since the Kayna case surfaced - 6,604 confirmed, 3,175 dead as of Sept 6, up from 6,342/3,072 three days earlier - with North Kivu alone now at 1,000 cases and 659 deaths. Health workers treating them have gone on strike multiple times over unpaid wages, a second breakdown layered on top of the surveillance gap that let the case through.
storylines.location: Kayna, North Kivu, Democratic Republic of Congo

history.note: The national count keeps climbing: 6,604 confirmed, 3,175 dead as of Sept 6 (up from 6,342/3,072), North Kivu alone at 1,000 cases/659 deaths. Health workers treating them have struck multiple times over unpaid wages.

A new Ebola case surfaced in rebel-held Kayna, North Kivu, in a patient who'd traveled from government-held Butembo - months after M23 declared the outbreak over in its territory. M23 has reimposed movement restrictions it had eased.

storylines.title: The US just signed a 100-year oil deal with a president nobody elected
storylines.observation: The US and Venezuela's acting president Delcy Rodríguez — installed after Washington removed Maduro in January — struck a deal granting a new joint venture 55% US-controlled ownership and 100-year rights to develop 65 billion barrels across 17 oil fields.
storylines.question: Does a resource deal's scale change what it means that neither government asked its own people first?
storylines.hidden_question: Is a 100-year contract a legitimate exercise of sovereignty, or a wager that whoever eventually contests it will no longer be in a position to matter?
storylines.pattern: a resource deal signed by an unelected government, at a scale built to outlast any successor who might contest it
storylines.why_now: The criticism has spread across Venezuela's own political spectrum: opposition figure Henrique Capriles is now publicly calling out "the opacity that has characterized the country's oil revenues," while Halliburton is reportedly nearing its own separate deal - meaning even critics of the process aren't positioned to stop more companies from joining it.

history.note: Opposition figure Henrique Capriles publicly criticized "the opacity that has characterized the country's oil revenues," as Halliburton reportedly nears its own separate Venezuela deal - critics of the process aren't positioned to stop more firms joining it.

Chevron put a specific figure on its separate expansion: $7B aimed at more than doubling its Venezuela output to roughly 600,000 barrels a day - a concrete number now sitting alongside the still-unresolved fight over the larger deal's legitimacy.

storylines.title: The idol built to be worshipped is also built to dissolve
storylines.observation: Ahead of Ganesh Chaturthi (Sept 14-25), Indian artisans are preparing clay idols as alternatives to Plaster of Paris versions now restricted in several cities — a ritual whose central object, designed for immersion, is colliding with what immersion does to rivers and lakes.
storylines.question: What happens to a ritual when the object at its center turns out to be the thing polluting the water it's offered to?
storylines.hidden_question: Is switching the idol's material preserving the tradition, or quietly replacing what the ritual actually was?
storylines.pattern: a traditional practice re-engineering its own central object to survive contact with modern environmental limits
storylines.why_now: Hyderabad's civic bodies are now supplying the alternative at scale, not just mandating it: GHMC, the state pollution board, and the metro development authority are together distributing nearly 475,000 free clay idols this week - answering the eco-idol tension with volume rather than restriction alone.

history.note: Hyderabad's GHMC, TGPCB and HMDA are together distributing nearly 475,000 free clay idols this week - the eco-idol tension now being answered with government-supplied volume, not just court-ordered restriction.

A Bombay High Court directive now requires Mumbai idols under 6 feet to immerse in artificial ponds, not the sea - the same eco-idol tension already active in Hyderabad has reached India's largest Ganeshotsav city, this time by court order.

storylines.title: A state tried to send fossil fuel companies a $75 billion bill. A federal judge just voided it
storylines.observation: A federal judge struck down New York's Climate Change Superfund Act, which sought to collect roughly $75 billion from fossil fuel companies for past emissions, ruling the state law is preempted by federal law and reaches into territory that belongs to Washington, not Albany.
storylines.question: Can any single state make a global industry pay for a global harm, or does the scale of the problem itself put the remedy out of a state's legal reach?
storylines.hidden_question: Is this ruling about federalism, or is it about which level of government is actually willing to send the bill?
storylines.pattern: a state-level remedy for a global-scale harm struck down for operating at the wrong scale of government
storylines.why_now: DOJ's own statement went further than the judge's reasoning, calling the law "unconstitutional" outright rather than just preempted - while state Sen. Liz Krueger, who co-sponsored the original bill, is now publicly telling the AG "we believe that we will win" on appeal. Both sides are already arguing the case a level up from where the judge actually left it.
storylines.location: Albany, New York / Northern District of New York

history.note: DOJ's statement called the law "unconstitutional," going further than the judge's narrower preemption ruling. State Sen. Liz Krueger, the bill's co-sponsor, is now telling the AG directly: "we believe that we will win" on appeal.

Climate advocates are publicly pressing AG Letitia James to appeal Judge Sannes' ruling, calling it "far from the last word." Hochul still hasn't committed either way, with the court's Sept 14 status-report deadline now less than two weeks out.

storylines.title: The emperor built his bathhouse inside the one part of the palace made for war
storylines.observation: Archaeologists uncovered a 1,700-year-old private bath complex — heated floors, three pools, a sauna, a domed ceiling with six windows — built inside a defensive tower at the fortified palace of Vrelo-Šarkamen in Serbia, once home to Roman emperor Maximinus Daza.
storylines.question: What does it mean to build the palace's most comfortable room inside the one part of it designed for defense?
storylines.hidden_question: Was hiding luxury inside a fortification a sign the emperor felt safe, or a sign he specifically didn't?
storylines.pattern: opulence deliberately built inside the structure meant to withstand attack
storylines.why_now: No follow-up reporting has surfaced since the initial find; going dormant as a single-note discovery rather than re-bumping it without anything new. Worth reactivating if the Institute of Archaeology publishes further findings on the site.

history.note: A 1,700-year-old bath complex - heated floors, three pools, a sauna - was found built into a defensive tower at emperor Maximinus Daza's palace in Serbia. Archaeologists say the tower-bath combination has no known parallel elsewhere in the empire.

storylines.title: Saturn grew a second hexagon, except it has ten sides
storylines.observation: Hubble has confirmed a huge ten-sided atmospheric wave encircling Saturn's south pole — the first large, regular-sided jet pattern ever observed in the planet's southern hemisphere, and a feature Cassini's 13 years in orbit never showed any sign of.
storylines.question: What does it mean for a stable, decades-old planetary feature to suddenly grow an entirely new counterpart?
storylines.hidden_question: Is this evidence the hexagon's mechanism was always latent at both poles, or evidence something about Saturn's atmosphere has actually changed?
storylines.pattern: a long-studied, presumed-stable phenomenon turning out to have an undiscovered twin
storylines.why_now: No follow-up reporting has surfaced since Hubble's initial confirmation; going dormant as a single-note research finding rather than re-bumping it without anything new. Worth reactivating if a follow-up observation campaign or new modeling of the feature emerges.

history.note: Hubble confirms a ten-sided atmospheric wave circling Saturn's south pole, tracing back to 2023 and still strengthening - the first large regular-sided jet pattern ever seen there, after decades of searches and 13 years of Cassini data showed nothing.

storylines.title: The tariffs everyone had two weeks to prepare for took effect anyway
storylines.observation: Canada's dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on more than 700 US goods took effect at 12:01am today, matching the US's own 50% tariff on $27.6 billion of Canadian goods - the negotiated-deal window both sides had two weeks to use closed without one.
storylines.question: What does advance notice actually buy two governments, if both sides let the deadline arrive anyway?
storylines.hidden_question: Was the two-week gap real negotiating time, or just a formality both sides always expected to expire?
storylines.pattern: a telegraphed deadline arriving exactly as threatened, despite weeks of visible opportunity to avoid it
storylines.why_now: Ottawa paired the tariffs with a C$7.5B domestic support package for the workers and businesses its own countermeasures will hit hardest - hedging against the retaliation it chose to impose anyway, rather than treating support and escalation as alternatives to each other.

history.note: Canada's retaliatory tariffs on 700+ US goods took effect at 12:01am, matching the US's 50% tariff on $27.6B of Canadian goods dollar-for-dollar - the two-week negotiation window both sides had closed without a deal.
